definition: A spoken dialog system (SDS) is a computer system able to converse with a human with voice.
details: It has two essential components that do not exist in a written text dialog system: a speech recognizer and a text-to-speech module (written text dialog systems usually use other input systems provided by an OS). It can be further distinguished from command and control speech systems that can respond to requests but do not attempt to maintain continuity over time.

explainer.lead: A spoken dialog system is a computer system able to converse with a human by voice. It matters because it adds two components absent from written text dialog systems: a speech recognizer and a text-to-speech module.

tiers.eli5: It's a computer you can talk to out loud, which listens, understands and answers back with a voice.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers combine speech recognition and text-to-speech with dialog handling to maintain a conversation over time. A pitfall is confusing it with command-and-control speech systems, which respond to requests but do not try to maintain continuity.
tiers.paperLevel: A system able to converse with a human with voice; it requires a speech recognizer and a text-to-speech module, which written text dialog systems typically lack. It is distinguished from command-and-control systems that do not attempt continuity over time.

explainer.example: A caller speaks a request, the recognizer transcribes it, and the system replies in synthesized speech while keeping track of the ongoing conversation.
